title: Don't Use a Cannon to Kill a Fly: Lightweight Model Editing for LLMs to Correct Deprecated API Recommendations
core_idea: Per-API layer importance scoring from gradient magnitudes separates common from API-specific layers before lightweight editing
baselines: Pre-edit; REPLACEAPI; ROME; MEMIT; PMET; AlphaEdit; GRACE; A-GRACE; MALMEN; FT-L; LoRA; AdaLoRA
metrics: Exact match (EM); API exact match (AEM); BLEU; ROUGE-L; editing time; peak memory; HumanEval Pass@1 (retained utility)
metrics_display: Exact match; API exact match; BLEU; ROUGE-L; editing time; peak memory
q1_assessment: The update requirement comes from documented API deprecations and repository code using their replacements. Editing targets are single-line API completions, with constructed rephrasings and alternative contexts used to evaluate generalization and portability.
q1_evidence: arXiv v2: Sec. 3.2 and Figs. 1-2 (PDF pp. 6-8) derive completion prompts from repository functions using current APIs, starting from 145 deprecated-to-current mappings across eight Python libraries. Generalization uses rephrased prompts; portability uses distinct contexts involving the same target API.
q2_assessment: The need for correction is directly established for the retained editing instances: the target model repeatedly recommends the deprecated API before editing. This supports targeted correction of observed obsolete recommendations in the evaluated models.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.2, Step 2 (PDF p. 6) retains a candidate only when the target model generates the deprecated API in all three greedy completions. Sec. 3.1 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 5, 8) identify the model-specific sets for Qwen2.5-Coder-3B, CodeGemma-2B and DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B; Tables 3-5 (PDF p. 10) report pre-edit results.
q3_assessment: Selected-layer editing improves specificity relative to AdaLoRA while retaining comparable effectiveness, generalization and portability in single-line reference agreement. Non-target completion checks and HumanEval provide separate preservation evidence; the target evaluation does not establish end-to-end functional correctness.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 9) defines EM, API Exact Match, BLEU and ROUGE-L. Table 6 and Sec. 4.3.2 (PDF pp. 12-13) compare AdaLoRA-L with AdaLoRA across the four dimensions. Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 7) defines non-target completion probes, and Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 13) reports retained HumanEval performance. Sec. 6 (PDF p. 17) explicitly limits target evaluation to single-line completion.

title: Model Editing for LLMs4Code: How Far Are We?
core_idea: Adds a contrastively trained MLP encoder to GRACE and uses mean-pooled token representations instead of the last token
baselines: FT-L; ROME; MEMIT; PMET; MALMEN; GRACE
metrics: Exact match (EM); BLEU; ROUGE-L; fluency (n-gram entropy); editing time; peak memory
metrics_display: Exact match; BLEU; ROUGE-L; n-gram entropy; editing time; peak memory
q1_assessment: The update targets are reference outputs in constructed code-generation and code-summarization editing tasks. CLMEEval derives its examples from existing datasets, rather than documented software changes or a per-instance screen of erroneous model outputs.
q1_evidence: Sec. III-C and Fig. 1 (PDF pp. 3-5) construct CNLE from CoNaLa and CSNE from CodeSearchNet, filtering source pairs and adding rewritten intents or variable-renamed code for generalization. Sec. III-F (PDF p. 6) applies editing to every target case regardless of whether the original model already produces the desired output.
q2_assessment: Original-model results establish low agreement with the prescribed references for CodeLlama, CodeQwen and StableCode. A small manual check supports semantic mismatches in sampled CodeLlama outputs, but the protocol does not establish a genuine functional defect for every edited instance.
q2_evidence: Sec. III-F and Table IV (PDF pp. 6-7) report unconditional editing and original-model reference-agreement scores. Sec. V (PDF p. 11) manually examines 50 CNLE cases whose CodeLlama outputs differ from the reference and finds semantic misalignment in 45; this check is limited to that model and sample.
q3_assessment: A-GRACE improves reference agreement on related inputs while retaining strong target agreement; these results do not establish executable correctness. Non-target output comparisons show model- and dataset-dependent preservation, including substantial specificity losses on CNLE. Generalization is limited to constructed variants, and fluency measures continuations from target and related inputs rather than broader retained coding capability.
q3_evidence: Secs. III-C to III-E (PDF pp. 4-5) define nearest-neighbor non-target probes, rewritten-input generalization, EM/BLEU/ROUGE-L and n-gram-entropy fluency. Sec. IV-C and Table VI (PDF pp. 9-10) compare A-GRACE with GRACE, showing generalization gains alongside sharply lower CNLE specificity and similar CSNE specificity. Sec. V (PDF p. 11) limits the study to two Python tasks.

title: ReCode: Updating Code API Knowledge with Reinforcement Learning
core_idea: Rule-based reinforcement fine-tuning with a format reward and AST-syntax-checked string-similarity reward
metrics: Pass@1; Pass@5; retained coding performance on HumanEval+
q1_assessment: Training requirements come from real library release information, used to construct old/new API-code pairs. The main update evaluation uses synthetic CodeUpdateArena tasks, so its evidence of adaptation concerns experimentally specified API changes.
q1_evidence: AAAI-26 version: Secs. 2-3.2 and Fig. 3 (PDF pp. 2-4) describe release-note collection, GPT-4 generation of migration pairs and expert review. The paper distinguishes these real training updates from the synthetic updates used in CodeUpdateArena evaluation.
q2_assessment: Untrained baselines show an adaptation gap on the evaluated tasks for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-Coder-v1.5-7B-Instruct, even with update information supplied. The evidence concerns benchmark task performance rather than a failure screen for every training example.
q2_evidence: Secs. 4.1-4.2 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-5) compare untrained, SFT and ReCode models on CodeUpdateArena. Sec. 4.1 (PDF p. 5) states that all tests provide updated information; Sec. 5.2 (PDF pp. 6-7) discusses failures in which the original model overlooks update information in the prompt.
q3_assessment: Execution-based Pass@k supports improved task performance with update documentation supplied, separately from the syntax-checked similarity used for training. HumanEval+ assesses retained general code-generation capability and shows smaller, but nonzero, losses relative to SFT.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 4) defines format and AST-syntax-checked string-similarity rewards. Secs. 3.1 and 4.1 (PDF pp. 3, 5) evaluate generated functions with CodeUpdateArena test cases. Table 1 and Sec. 4.2 (PDF p. 5) report higher Pass@1/5 after ReCode and the separate before/after HumanEval+ results.

title: Neuron Patching: Semantic-based Neuron-level Language Model Repair for Code Generation
core_idea: Attributes neuron scores then estimates patches that pull representations from the argmax semantic basis toward the target basis
metrics: Exact match (EM); edit similarity; BLEU; ROUGE-L; updated-neuron cost; elapsed-time cost; accuracy change (dAcc); mean absolute error (MAE) of probability-gap changes; root mean square error (RMSE) of probability-gap changes; update footprint (patch coefficient times updated-neuron cost)
benchmark: CoNaLa; IA32; TLDR; HumanEval; BigCodeBench-hard; handcrafted generalization and specificity probes
metrics_display: Exact match; edit similarity; BLEU / ROUGE-L; accuracy change; probability-gap change; neuron and time cost
q1_assessment: Repair requirements primarily come from mismatches between predicted and reference tokens in code-generation datasets. The side-effect benchmark imposes artificial token substitutions, while a separate nonexistent-API example illustrates a concrete model failure.
q1_evidence: Secs. 4.1-4.2 (PDF pp. 11-12) define patch cases using reference-token mismatches in CoNaLa, IA32, TLDR, HumanEval and BigCodeBench-hard. Sec. 4.3 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 13-14) prescribe operator, keyword and API-token substitutions. Sec. 6.2 and Fig. 7 (PDF pp. 21-22) correct CodeGen-2B's nonexistent distance.manhattan() call to distance.cityblock().
q2_assessment: Conditional mismatch checking and pre-edit results establish reference-token prediction gaps in CodeGen-2B, StarCoder2-3B and CodeLlama-7B. These gaps justify the tested token corrections, but aggregate reference disagreement alone does not establish that the generated program is functionally wrong.
q2_evidence: Algorithm 1 (PDF p. 5) initiates patching when the predicted token differs from the supplied target. Secs. 4.1-4.2 (PDF pp. 11-12) use each inference example as a patch set and validate it on the same data. Tables 4-5 (PDF pp. 15-16) report pre-repair reference-agreement scores for short- and long-code tasks.
q3_assessment: The experiments support improved reference agreement and target-token preference, including long-code tasks; they do not establish functional correctness through execution. Generalization and specificity are supported by separate token-substitution probes and the API case, rather than a broad retained-capability test. Successive-repair examples also expose incomplete repairs and interference with previously correct predictions.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4 (PDF pp. 10-11) defines token exact match, BLEU/ROUGE and probability-gap measures; Tables 4-5 (PDF pp. 15-16) report gains, including HumanEval and BigCodeBench-hard. Sec. 4.3 and Table 8 (PDF pp. 13-14, 19) evaluate related versus unrelated substitution probes. Secs. 6.1-6.2, Table 9 and Fig. 7 (PDF pp. 20-22) show both API generalization/specificity and regressions under successive repairs.

title: CREME: Robustness Enhancement of Code LLMs via Layer-Aware Model Editing
core_idea: Locates the layer most sensitive to perturbation then aligns perturbed and clean hidden representations there
metrics: Pass@1; Generalized Relative Improvement Ratio (G-RIR); localization time; editing time; testing time
metrics_display: Pass@1; generalized relative improvement ratio; localization, editing and testing time
q1_assessment: The update requirement is demonstrated loss of functional correctness under prompt perturbations. Evaluation prompts are constructed from HumanEval and MBPP using a taxonomy informed by practitioner observations, so the setting represents controlled prompt variation rather than naturally collected developer failures.
q1_evidence: Sec. 4.2 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 5-6) construct HumanEval-R and MBPP-R using NLPerturbator with 20 lexical and syntactic perturbation types. Sec. 2.1 and Fig. 1 (PDF p. 2) illustrate a CodeLlama solution that passes tests for the clean prompt but fails after typographical changes.
q2_assessment: The need for correction is directly established for the retained, model-specific perturbation-sensitive examples. Before editing, CodeLlama-7b and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B show a substantial execution-based accuracy drop relative to the corresponding clean prompts.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4.2 (PDF p. 5) measures test-based pass rates before editing and retains examples only when the clean-to-perturbed robustness drop is at least 0.3. Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 6) identifies the two models; Table 2 (PDF p. 7) reports clean and perturbed base-model Pass@1.
q3_assessment: Execution-based results support improved functional correctness on perturbed prompts and transfer to held-out tasks within the same perturbation type. Cross-type transfer is additionally tested in one model/dataset setting. Clean-input tests support largely retained coding performance within HumanEval and MBPP, with applicability limited to the evaluated models and perturbation taxonomy.
q3_evidence: Secs. 4.3-4.4 (PDF pp. 5-6) define test-based Pass@1, G-RIR and leave-one-in editing. Tables 2-4 (PDF pp. 7-8) report held-out robustness gains; Table 5 (PDF p. 8) tests C3 edits on other types for HumanEval/QwenCoder. Sec. 6.1 and Table 7 (PDF pp. 9-10) evaluate clean-data Pass@1/10 after 40 sampled edits per configuration. Sec. 6.4 (PDF p. 10) states model and perturbation-scope limitations.

title: Mitigating Package Hallucinations in Large Language Models via Model Editing
core_idea: Locates attention and feed-forward modules by package-validity risk and optimizes boundary-aware LoRA adapters while freezing backbone weights
metrics: Sample-level hallucination rate (Sample-HR); package-level hallucination rate (Package-HR); valid-package response rate (Valid-Rate); Pass@1; Pass@10; retained coding performance on HumanEval; localization time; editing time; testing time; artifact size
benchmark: Model-specific high-risk package recommendation prompts; HumanEval
metrics_display: Sample-level hallucination rate; package-level hallucination rate; valid-package response rate; Pass@1/10; time; artifact size
q1_assessment: The update requirement comes from observed invalid package recommendations under a PyPI availability and model-cutoff rule. The prompts are LLM-generated from descriptions of popular Python packages, so the failures are observed in a constructed package-recommendation setting.
q1_evidence: Sec. IV-A (PDF p. 5) uses the recent Python subset of Spracklen et al.'s generated prompt dataset, derived from package descriptions. It labels a package valid only if it exists on PyPI with a release before the model's knowledge cutoff; extracted valid and hallucinated names define the edit cases.
q2_assessment: Model-specific screening directly establishes recurring package hallucinations for the retained prompts in DeepSeekCoder, Qwen3 and Llama-3.1. This supports correction of demonstrated failures within the selected high-risk prompt sets.
q2_evidence: Sec. IV-A and Table I (PDF p. 5) query each model five times and retain prompts with Sample-HR greater than 0.5, then split them into four independent 50-prompt edit subsets and an unseen evaluation set. Sec. IV-D (PDF p. 6) identifies the evaluated models, and Table II (PDF p. 7) reports unedited hallucination rates.
q3_assessment: Results support reduced invalid package generation on edited and unseen prompts, with cross-task transfer to code and pip-install recommendations. Valid-Rate assesses preservation of valid package output, and HumanEval separately assesses retained coding capability, with some model-dependent losses. Package existence does not establish task suitability or functional correctness of the generated target code.
q3_evidence: Sec. IV-C (PDF p. 6) defines Sample-HR, Package-HR and Valid-Rate, explicitly separating existence from task suitability. Table II (PDF p. 7) reports target/unseen results. Sec. V-B and Table III (PDF pp. 7-8) check extracted dependencies on 100 unseen prompts per model across two other tasks, without executing the generated target code. Sec. VI-B and Table VI (PDF p. 9) report before/after HumanEval Pass@1/10 across four edited versions.

title: Understanding Robustness of Model Editing in Code LLMs
core_idea: Shows execution-based metrics contradict similarity-based ones because code admits workarounds
baselines: FT-L; GRACE; A-GRACE; MALMEN; MEMIT; PMET; ROME
metrics: Compiles@k; Pass@k; Successful Adoption@k; Workaround@k; Shapley compilation contribution (phiC); Shapley post-compilation contribution (phiQ); compilation-attributed degradation share (CF)
metrics_display: Compiles@k; Pass@k; Successful Adoption@k; Workaround@k; compilation and post-compilation contributions
q1_assessment: The update requirement is imposed experimentally through synthetic changes to API names, parameters and return types in established coding tasks. The study therefore evaluates adaptation to artificial specifications rather than actual library releases.
q1_evidence: arXiv v2: Sec. 3.1, Tables 2-3 (PDF pp. 3-4) and Appendix A (PDF p. 13) construct instances from APPS, HumanEval and MBPP. Five API-modification types transform canonical API calls into the new edit targets.
q2_assessment: The need for adaptation follows from the imposed API changes, with pre-edit reliance on the target API checked for the filtered generalization subset. This establishes relevance to the synthetic update rather than a naturally occurring model failure.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 3) defines the edit target by modifying the API call in a canonical solution. Sec. 5.2 (PDF p. 6) retains generalization problems whose pre-edit model generation also uses that target API, allowing subsequent adoption to be distinguished from workaround behavior.
q3_assessment: The experiments support the reported limitations of existing editors: passing task tests can coexist with workaround behavior, and generalization and non-target performance can deteriorate under successive edits. Functional tests, adoption diagnostics and specificity tasks assess distinct aspects of the update.
q3_evidence: Secs. 3.3-4 (PDF pp. 4-5) define execution checks, Pass@k, Successful Adoption@k and Workaround@k. Sec. 5.2 and Table 5 (PDF p. 6) separate adoption from test-passing workarounds. Secs. 5.1 and 5.4, Tables 4 and 7 (PDF pp. 5-8) evaluate generalization and tasks involving unmodified APIs under single and successive edits, reporting substantial degradation in multiple configurations.

title: CodeUpdateArena: Benchmarking Knowledge Editing on API Updates
core_idea: Synthesizes API updates with program-synthesis tasks so editing is scored by execution rather than string match
metrics: UPass@k; SPass@k (retained coding performance on HumanEval); Pass@k with updated API
q1_assessment: The benchmark experimentally constructs atomic API updates and associated program-synthesis tasks. These requirements isolate adaptation to artificial API specifications; the updates themselves are not taken from actual software releases.
q1_evidence: arXiv v3: Sec. 1 (PDF p. 2) motivates synthetic updates as a way to reduce pretraining contamination. Secs. 4.1-4.2 and Fig. 2 (PDF pp. 4-6) describe GPT-4 generation of update specifications, implementations, tests and synthesis tasks, followed by execution checks and manual filtering.
q2_assessment: Unedited-model baselines establish limited ability to apply the newly specified APIs on the benchmark tasks. This is evidence of an adaptation gap within the controlled synthetic setting.
q2_evidence: Sec. 6.1 (PDF p. 7) identifies GPT-4, Claude-3.5, CodeLlama and the two DeepSeek-Coder models. Table 4 (PDF p. 8) reports low base-model UPass@k despite higher ordinary Pass@k in the updated environment. Sec. 3 (PDF p. 4) explains that a solution can pass tests without depending on the new API.
q3_assessment: Execution tests support update-dependent program synthesis, and training on program-synthesis examples improves this outcome in the edited models without requiring update documentation at inference. HumanEval-based SPass assesses broader capability retention and reveals model-dependent trade-offs, rather than guaranteeing unchanged behavior for each unaffected API.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3 (PDF p. 4) requires a UPass solution to pass all tests with the updated API and fail at least one with the old API. Sec. 6.1 (PDF pp. 7-8) describes single-edit evaluation, held-out synthesis examples and SPass on sampled HumanEval tasks. Table 4 and Sec. 6.2 (PDF pp. 8-9) report FT(PS) gains in UPass alongside model-dependent changes in SPass.

title: CodeSync: Synchronizing LLMs with Dynamic Code Evolution at Scale
core_idea: Mines real API signature changes and synthesizes paired legacy and updated invocations for completion, correction, and multiple-choice evaluation
metrics: BLEU; ROUGE-L; relative edit distance (RED); CodeBLEU; multiple-choice answer success (Pass@1/3/5); retained coding Pass@1 on HumanEval; HumanEval retention ratio; training time
metrics_display: BLEU / CodeBLEU; ROUGE-L; relative edit distance; answer success; retained coding Pass@1; training time
q1_assessment: The underlying update requirements are real API signature changes across library versions. The benchmark uses repository contexts but synthesizes paired legacy/updated invocations and evaluation questions, so its tasks represent constructed applications of those changes.
q1_evidence: ICML 2025 version: Secs. 2.1-2.4, Tables 1-2 and Figs. 3-4 (PDF pp. 3-5) compare signatures across six Python libraries, retrieve GitHub invocation contexts and use DeepSeek-V3 to construct legacy/updated calls. The resulting tasks ask models to complete, correct or recognize updated invocations.
q2_assessment: Original-model evaluations establish limited performance on the constructed updated-API tasks in the five models used for updating. A legacy-reference comparison for the two Qwen models further supports an update-related gap at benchmark level.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.2 and Table 4 (PDF p. 7) report Original results for all five update subjects on completion, correction and multiple-choice tasks. The fine-grained analysis and Table 5 (PDF pp. 7-8) compare Qwen2.5 and Qwen2.5-Coder against legacy-reference answers and find higher scores than against updated references.
q3_assessment: Changes in reference agreement and multiple-choice accuracy support partial adaptation to updated invocations. These target-task metrics do not establish functional correctness; HumanEval separately assesses retained general code-generation capability.
q3_evidence: Sec. 2.4 (PDF pp. 5-6) uses BLEU, ROUGE-L, relative edit distance and CodeBLEU for completion/correction, while MCQ Pass@k measures correct answer selection. Sec. 3.2 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 7-8) report updating results and retained HumanEval performance. Appendix D.2.2 (PDF p. 25) describes the general code-generation evaluation; these HumanEval tests assess retained utility rather than execution of the requested API updates.

title: A Semantic-based Optimization Approach for Repairing LLMs: Case Study on Code Generation
core_idea: Locates buggy neurons, solves semantic analytical patches, and applies shortest-path planning to repair code LMs without full retraining
metrics: Exact match; BLEU; repair accuracy; time cost; relative performance drop (RPD) on held-out CoNaLa; degradation percentage; mean absolute error (MAE) of probability-gap changes; root mean square error (RMSE) of probability-gap changes; Generalization-Specificity Harmonic score (GSH)
metrics_display: Exact match; BLEU; repair accuracy; relative performance drop; generalization-specificity scores; time cost
q1_assessment: Reference-token mismatches in existing coding datasets define the repair target, while a separate benchmark inherited from MINT supplies controlled targets for side-effect analysis. These requirements concern generation-behavior repair against prescribed references rather than documented software changes or independently verified program defects.
q1_evidence: Sec. 2.1 (PDF p. 2) defines a model failure as disagreement between the argmax token and the reference target token. Sec. 4.3 and Table 2 (PDF pp. 6-7) identify CoNaLa, IA32 and TLDR, the 450-example side-effect benchmark inherited from MINT, and HumanEval/BigCodeBench-hard for long-code repair.
q2_assessment: Pre-repair predictions establish reference-token mismatches in the five evaluated code LMs, and repairs are validated against the same target data. This establishes the stated next-token correction need, but a reference mismatch alone does not establish a functional defect.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4, RQ1 setup (PDF p. 5) uses the same example to repair and validate a failure. Sec. 4.2, Table 1 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 6-7) identify the five models and report unmodified-model ExactMatch/BLEU alongside repaired results; Table 7 (PDF p. 10) provides corresponding pre-repair results for the two Qwen2.5-Coder models on long-code tasks.
q3_assessment: The experiments support improved target-token/reference agreement in single- and multiple-failure repair, including long-code tasks, without establishing functional correctness through execution. Held-out CoNaLa BLEU and related/unrelated-input probability-gap probes provide separate retention, generalization and specificity evidence within their tested models and datasets, with model-dependent trade-offs.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4 (PDF pp. 5-6) defines same-example repair validation, ExactMatch/BLEU, the 80/20 hold-out test, and probability-gap MAE/RMSE and GSH. Tables 3 and 7 (PDF pp. 7, 10) report reference-agreement gains, including HumanEval/BigCodeBench-hard. Table 5 (PDF p. 8) reports small held-out CoNaLa BLEU drops for Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B. Sec. 4.3 and Table 6 (PDF pp. 7, 10) use nine related and fourteen unrelated probes per edit and report generalization-specificity trade-offs for CodeLlama, StarCoder2 and OpenCoder.

title: Diagnosing Knowledge Gaps in LLM Tool Use: An Agentic Benchmark for Novel API Acquisition
core_idea: Dynamically discovers novel APIs per base model, decomposes knowledge bundles, and diagnoses failures across six categories comparing RAG vs parametric adaptation
baselines: RAG (knowledge components); SFT; RAFT; GRACE; MEMIT; AlphaEdit; no-knowledge baseline
metrics: Pass@1; Pass@5; API-selection accuracy; parameter correctness (AST keyword-argument match rate); semantic-equivalence judge score; failure-category distribution
metrics_display: Pass@1/5; API-selection accuracy; parameter correctness; semantic-equivalence score; failure categories
q1_assessment: The underlying requirements come from real API additions identified across library releases relative to a target model's knowledge cutoff. Coding tasks and knowledge bundles are generated for these APIs, so the benchmark studies constructed applications of real new interfaces rather than naturally occurring developer requests.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.1-3.2 and Fig. 1 (PDF pp. 3-5) compare public API surfaces in releases before and after the model cutoff, extract signatures/examples/mechanism information, and generate three difficulty-graded tasks per API. Appendix B.1 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 13-14) document the actual version pairs used for the primary Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct benchmark.
q2_assessment: Model-conditional failure filtering directly establishes an initial capability gap on retained tasks, with no-knowledge baselines confirming low unaided performance. This evidence is tied to the selected model and generated task pool, especially the primary Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct setting.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.2, Stage 4 (PDF p. 5) requires the reference to pass and the target model without API knowledge to fail at least two of three sampled completions. Sec. 4.1 and Fig. 2 (PDF pp. 5-6) report 3.1% no-knowledge Pass@1 on 1,386 tasks for the primary model; Sec. 4.4 and Table 1 (PDF p. 8) report the unupdated baseline for the separate parametric-adaptation test split.
q3_assessment: Execution tests requiring the target API support improved API use with supplied knowledge, while bundle-stripped probes show limited internalization under the tested adaptation budget. Leave-diffusers-out evaluation supports partial cross-library transfer but exposes persistent import failures. Preservation of unrelated behavior or general coding capability is not separately evaluated after updating.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF p. 5) couples executable assertions with a target-API spy to reject bypasses. Sec. 4.4, Tables 1-2 and Fig. 5 (PDF pp. 7-9) compare updating with/without knowledge bundles and report reduced Pass@1 with diffusers held out despite relatively stable API selection. Appendix E.5 (PDF p. 30) specifies the 123-task bundle-stripped subset of the 399-task test split. Appendix A (PDF p. 13) limits the internalization finding to the tested post-hoc adaptation budget and single-API Python tasks; these evaluations do not include a separate non-target retention set.

title: Environment-Aware Code Generation: How far are We?
target: Environment-specific executable code under explicit library versions
core_idea: Introduces VersiBCB for multi-package executable code generation under explicit library versions and explores RAG, LoRA-MoE, and memory-augmented adaptation
base_models: DeepSeek-Coder-7B; CodeGemma-7B-it; CodeLlama-13B; StarCoder2-15B; LLaMA3-70B; GPT-4.1-mini; DeepSeek-v3; GPT-4o-mini; GPT-4.1-nano; Gemini-1.5-flash-002; GPT-3.5-turbo; LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct
baselines: Unadapted base model; RAG; LoRA-MoE; Memory-augmented generation
metrics: Pass@1; Pass@3; Pass@5; weighted Pass@1 (wPass@1); strict Pass@1 (Strict@1); lenient Pass@1 (Lenient@1)
metrics_display: Pass@1/3/5; weighted Pass@1; strict Pass@1; lenient Pass@1
q1_assessment: Real library versions and cross-version incompatibilities supply the update requirements. VersiBCB constructs generation and migration instances by traversing feasible package-version combinations around BigCodeBench examples and repairing version-sensitive code, providing controlled instances of real compatibility requirements.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.1 and 3.1, Figs. 1-2 (PDF pp. 2-3) define explicit multi-package environments and source-to-target migration, then traverse library versions until reference code fails through deprecation, signature changes or behavioral divergence. A reflection-guided agent repairs code and tests; Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 3-4) distinguishes strict and lenient deprecation policies.
q2_assessment: Unadapted-model results establish aggregate gaps in environment-aware generation and migration, including the LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct baseline used for adaptation. The strict/lenient comparison additionally shows reliance on deprecated APIs in the selected deprecation subset; instances are not individually screened for a failure by every evaluated model.
q2_evidence: Sec. 3.4 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 4-5) report low execution-based Pass@k for unadapted models. Sec. 5.1 and Table 6 (PDF p. 6) give the adaptation baseline's Pass@1 as 14.63% for generation and 42.51% for migration. Sec. 5.2 and Table 7 (PDF p. 7) show gaps between strict and lenient Pass@1 when deprecated alternatives remain callable.
q3_assessment: Unit tests in specified environments support modest, strategy-dependent gains in generation and migration; strict versus lenient scoring separately assesses deprecated-API avoidance. Perturbed-version evaluation provides bounded compositional-generalization evidence and reveals MoE regressions. No separate post-adaptation evaluation establishes preservation of unrelated APIs or general coding capability.
q3_evidence: Sec. 5.1 and Table 6 (PDF p. 6) distinguish all-tests-passed Pass@1 from partial-test wPass@1. Sec. 5.2 and Table 7 (PDF p. 7) require active APIs for Strict@1. Sec. 5.3 and Table 8 (PDF pp. 7-8) perturb library versions while retaining executable references/tests, reporting mixed transfer and lower MoE success than baseline. The HumanEval+/LiveCodeBench comparison in Sec. 3.4 and Table 4 (PDF pp. 4-5) characterizes unadapted models rather than retained capability after customization.

title: Understanding and Improving Model Editing for Secure Code Generation
core_idea: First systematic empirical study of model editing for secure code generation; evaluates UltraEdit/DINM/DEFER* vs CoSec and proposes SafeEdit, a post-edit refinement combining functional tuning with edit-aware regularization
base_models: LLaMA-3.1-8B; LLaMA-3.2-3B; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B; CodeGen-6B; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; Qwen2.5-Coder-3B; StarCoder-3B; StarCoder-7B
metrics: Security ratio (SR); Pass@1; Pass@5; Pass@10; Secure@1-Pass; Secure-Pass@1; TradeOff; training and editing time; inference latency
edited_models: LLaMA-3.1-8B; LLaMA-3.2-3B; DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B; CodeGen-6B; Qwen2.5-Coder-7B; Qwen2.5-Coder-3B; StarCoder-3B; StarCoder-7B
metrics_display: Security ratio; Pass@1/5/10; joint security-correctness; TradeOff; editing time; inference latency
q1_assessment: The security-hardening requirement comes from vulnerable/fixed function pairs and CWE-based evaluation scenarios. Editing instances are constructed from vulnerability-relevant prefixes and secure suffixes; SafeEdit's subsequent functional refinement responds to the experimentally observed security-correctness trade-off.
q1_evidence: Secs. 2.2 and 2.5.1, Fig. 1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 4-5) construct 710 editing instances from vulnerable/fixed Python and C/C++ function pairs covering nine CWEs. Sec. 3.3 and Table 4 (PDF p. 10) show general programming regressions after hardening; Sec. 3.4 (PDF p. 11) motivates functional tuning with edit-aware regularization from those regressions.
q2_assessment: Vanilla-model security ratios establish insecure generation in the evaluated CWE scenarios, and before/after HumanEval results establish the functional regression motivating refinement. The editing set deliberately includes already-secure outputs, so the need is demonstrated at the model/scenario level rather than by a failure screen for every edit.
q2_evidence: Sec. 2.2 (PDF p. 5) explicitly applies the complete editing set regardless of whether each original completion is insecure, enabling cross-model comparison and regression analysis. Secs. 2.6-2.7 (PDF pp. 6-7) define CodeQL-based Security Ratio over valid, deduplicated completions. Table 2 (PDF p. 8) reports vanilla security baselines, while Table 4 (PDF p. 10) compares vanilla and edited HumanEval Pass@k.
q3_assessment: Security ratios and CodeGuard+'s joint security-and-test-passing metric support improved secure generation under the evaluated analyzers and tasks. HumanEval and MultiPL-E separately assess general coding retention: SafeEdit improves the overall trade-off and largely retains editing gains, but preservation is not uniform across models. Prompt perturbations and unseen-CWE tests provide bounded generalization evidence; SafeEdit's unseen-CWE refinement comparison covers two LLaMA models.
q3_evidence: Secs. 2.5.2-2.7 (PDF pp. 6-7) separate CWE security checks from HumanEval execution. Tables 2-4 (PDF pp. 8-10) report perturbation robustness, unseen-CWE transfer and functional regressions. Sec. 3.4.1 and Table 6 (PDF pp. 12-13) report SafeEdit's security/utility results, including the remaining Qwen2.5-Coder-7B HumanEval loss. Sec. 3.4.2 and Table 8 (PDF p. 13) combine CodeQL/SonarQube with unit tests on CodeGuard+. Secs. 4.2-4.3 and Tables 10-11 (PDF pp. 14-15) test unseen CWEs on two LLaMA models and retained MultiPL-E capability across eight models. Sec. 4.11 (PDF pp. 18-19) treats security ratios as static-analysis proxies, not security guarantees.
